Only Kotak covers SAMHI Hotels in the local library, maintaining a Buy with a PT of ₹240 (May 2026). The report acknowledges a difficult FY2026 — revenues of ₹12.5 bn (+10% yoy) and EBITDA of ₹4.3 bn (+6% yoy) at the full-year level, but 4QFY26 was weak, with EBITDA declining 8% yoy to ₹1.1 bn and margins contracting 575 bps. Multiple disruptions — the West Asia conflict dampening inbound tourism and a GST adjustment — hit the quarter hard. With a single house, there is no cross-house tension to triangulate.

My own read: SAMHI is a leveraged roll-up hospitality play in India's branded mid-market and upscale segment, converting independent hotels to brand-affiliated properties (Hyatt, Marriott, IHG) and capturing the yield uplift from rebranding and renovation. The structural tailwind is genuine — Indian hospitality is in a multi-year upcycle driven by rising domestic travel and limited quality supply additions. The problem is that SAMHI carries significant net debt, and FY2026's string of one-offs exposed the margin fragility of an asset-heavy, leveraged operator: when occupancy or RevPAR softens even briefly, PAT swings sharply. Kotak's Buy at ₹240 requires a clean FY2027 — no further disruptions and successful digestion of the capital programme. I'd be more cautious: the debt load makes the stock acutely sensitive to RevPAR disappointment, and if FY2027 delivers another year of execution noise, the downside to EV/EBITDA multiples from current debt levels is material. The two things I'd watch most: (1) RevPAR trajectory at the branded properties in Q1FY27 (seasonally weak — any positive surprise here would be a genuine signal); (2) whether the GST adjustment is fully resolved and non-recurring, or signals a structural cost.

Kotak|260524.change: PT data appears anomalous in the source file (prev: ₹4,823 → curr: ₹240 — almost certainly a parsing artefact, not a real cut); Buy maintained.
Kotak|260524.view:
Kotak is a constructive holder of this story, framing FY2026 as a year of unusual disruptions rather than structural deterioration. The headline numbers — full-year revenue +10% yoy, EBITDA +6% yoy — are respectable given the headwinds, but the 4Q miss (EBITDA −8% yoy, margins −575 bps) is harder to wave away.

The bull case rests on normalisation: if the West Asia disruption fades, the GST overhang clears, and the property conversion pipeline delivers RevPAR uplift, the EBITDA trajectory re-accelerates and the leverage starts looking manageable. That is a credible base case in a benign macro environment. What I would stress-test is the debt serviceability if FY2027 RevPAR growth disappoints — SAMHI does not have the balance-sheet cushion to absorb a second consecutive year of margin compression without equity risk rising. Kotak's Buy is defensible if you believe the disruptions were genuinely one-off; I would want to see Q1FY27 occupancy data before fully endorsing that view.

SJVN.summary:
Only CLSA covers SJVN in the local library, with a Hold and a PT cut from ₹90 to ₹72 (May 2026). The message is unambiguous: after aggressive capacity additions across thermal and variable renewable energy (VRE), SJVN is in a consolidation phase, with both new segments generating losses — VRE subsidiary ₹2.6 bn loss on climate and start-up challenges, thermal ₹930 mn loss on fuel logistics — pulling consolidated 4Q PAT to a ₹3.3 bn loss. CLSA sees no near-term re-rating catalyst. With only one house, there is no competing bull view to weigh.

My own read: SJVN's story has shifted from a sleepy Himalayan hydro PSU to an ambitious multi-energy conglomerate — but the execution has been messy. The original franchise (Nathpa Jhakri and Rampur hydro, long-tenure PPAs with HP and HPSEB) remains sound: captive low-cost generation with predictable cash flows. The problem is that management pivoted hard into thermal (Buxar, Bihar — 1,320 MW) and large-scale solar/wind, taking on substantial debt to chase the capacity-addition narrative that re-rated NTPC and other PSU power names. Those new plants are now loss-making, leverage has risen materially, and climate variability is disrupting renewable output. CLSA's Hold at ₹72 reflects a fair de-rating: the PSU premium that once justified a 2x P/BV has eroded as the consolidated return profile deteriorates. I would be cautious about even the Hold if VRE and thermal losses persist into FY2027 — at that point the consolidated PAT trajectory turns negative and the equity story breaks. The two things I'd watch most: (1) PLF at Buxar thermal — if fuel logistics normalise post-monsoon, the loss should narrow sharply and provide a first signal that the worst is priced in; (2) whether SJVN Green Energy Limited (SLL) requires a fresh capital infusion, which would signal deeper structural losses and be equity-dilutive at the parent level.

CLSA|260519.view:
CLSA's Hold is measured and well-grounded: the PT cut reflects the de-rating from rising losses at new capacities, but the analyst stops short of a Sell, likely because the core hydro franchise still generates stable cash and the PSU backstop provides a floor valuation. The framing — 'consolidation after excessive leverage' — is diplomatically accurate.

What I think CLSA is not fully pricing in: the structural risk that the VRE and thermal expansions were sized for a capital-markets re-rating story, not for shareholder returns. If PLFs at the VRE plants remain depressed by climate variability, the operating leverage works in reverse — fixed costs against disappointing generation — and the 'start-up challenges' never fully resolve. The Hold is appropriate for a passive holder who owns the hydro franchise and is waiting to see if the new segments self-correct; an active investor should want to see at least two consecutive quarters of loss-narrowing before adding exposure. I'd discount any near-term earnings recovery guidance from management given the track record on the new plants.

Samvardhana Motherson.summary:
The four-to-one bull-bear split is unusually clean. **JPMorgan**, **Nomura**, **CLSA**, and **Jefferies** are all Outperform/Buy with targets bunched ₹145–₹173 (CLSA ₹173, Jefferies ₹160, Nomura ₹155, JPMorgan ₹145); **Kotak** stands alone with a Sell at ₹120. Post the 4QFY26 beat, JP raised ₹135→₹145, Nomura raised ₹140→₹155, and Kotak — notably — raised ₹110→₹120 while keeping Sell, signalling less conviction in the bear case even as they hold it. The real fault line is non-auto durability vs wiring-harness margin headwinds: CLSA's ₹173 assumes 13% organic CAGR through FY28 on ASEAN + emerging-business momentum; Kotak's pushback is that elevated oil prices keep harness margins under pressure and the non-auto ramp is being valued at a premium before it's earned at scale.

My own read: SAMIL is executing better on diversification than the sell-side expected — consumer electronics 7.5x YoY and aerospace +40% aren't noise. That said, the wiring harness core (~55–60% of revenue) faces a slow structural drag as BEV platforms move to simpler, lower-value harnesses, and SAMIL's largest revenue base is Europe where auto demand is fragile. The market is already pricing the non-auto ramp at a meaningful premium; if consumer electronics is concentrated in one handset OEM program, supply-chain reshoring could stall. I'd land closer to Jefferies' ₹160 than CLSA's ₹173 — the growth rate is credible but the ₹173 requires both non-auto scale AND auto recovery simultaneously. The single variable I'd watch hardest is non-auto revenue share quarter-by-quarter: once it crosses 25% of consolidated with acceptable margins, the re-rating story is self-sustaining; if consumer electronics plateaus in FY27, valuations at 35x+ become difficult to defend.

JP|260521.view: JPMorgan's ₹10 raise is measured relative to its bull peers — they're upgrading estimates on the emerging-businesses beat rather than extrapolating aggressively. The OW at ₹145 implies roughly 10–12× EV/EBITDA on FY27, which is fair rather than stretched. JPMorgan's framing — revenue momentum driven by consumer electronics and integrated assemblies — correctly identifies the thesis but conservatively sizes it. I'd trust this call more than the higher targets: JPMorgan tends to anchor on realistic execution paths, and the ₹145 leaves room to be surprised on the upside without demanding perfection.

Nomura|260521.view: Nomura's ₹15 raise reflects genuine conviction; a 21% EBITDA beat above consensus earns a revision, not just a maintain. The "strong growth outlook driven by non-auto" title is well-chosen — they're pivoting the investment case away from auto-cycle sensitivity toward a structural mix-shift story. The ₹155 target is defensible if EBITDA margins hold at 10–11%: achievable if non-auto (higher-margin) continues to grow faster than the wiring harness segment. One thing I'd push back on: 4Q EBITDA margins sometimes carry a seasonal tailwind; confirming the 11% level in 1QFY27 will be the first real test of whether the margin improvement is structural.

CLSA|260520.change: Outperform maintained at ₹173; no prior TP on record to compare.
CLSA|260520.view: CLSA at ₹173 is the most aggressive target in the group, and the 13% organic CAGR through FY28 driven by ASEAN + emerging businesses is the critical assumption. The ASEAN angle is underweighted by other brokers — Motherson has been quietly building India-assembly and Southeast Asia exposure, and if OEM localisation mandates accelerate in those markets, CLSA's forecast could prove conservative. However, at ₹173, CLSA is pricing execution on multiple vectors simultaneously (non-auto scale, ASEAN ramp, harness margin stability). I'd use ₹173 as an optimistic scenario rather than base case — directionally right thesis, but demanding on precision of execution.

Jeff|260520.view: Jefferies holding its ₹160 target unchanged despite a 19% EBITDA beat is a sign of prior-period confidence, not laziness — they had already priced in execution. The 26% EPS CAGR over FY26–28 is the boldest earnings growth forecast of the group and is internally consistent: if non-auto reaches 25%+ of revenue at higher margins while auto volumes recover even modestly, the CAGR math works. Jefferies' Buy at ₹160 is probably the most defensible single target — not the most optimistic, but the one with the clearest earnings-derivation logic. The title ("growing well despite subdued macro") captures the key differentiator: SAMIL is decoupling from the auto-volume cycle, which is the core re-rating driver.

Kotak|260520.view: Kotak raising its Sell target by ₹10 while keeping the rating is an unusual move — it signals that even the bears couldn't ignore the beat, but they're not ready to capitulate on the margin-pressure thesis. The oil-price/wiring-harness argument has real merit: PVC and copper-derivative costs directly hit harness profitability, and if crude reverses the 2023–24 tailwind, Kotak's caution is vindicated. That said, at ₹120 with four peers setting targets ₹40–53 higher, Kotak is implicitly saying the non-auto mix shift is worth nothing — which seems too harsh given the 4Q evidence. I'd expect a Neutral revision from Kotak within two quarters if non-auto revenues sustain; the Sell at ₹120 is increasingly a structural-concern call rather than a near-term earnings call.

Sansera Engineering.summary:
Only **Nomura** covers Sansera in the current library, with a Buy at ₹3,114. The 4QFY26 print was a genuine beat — EBITDA margin 19.3% vs consensus 17.4%, revenue +28% YoY — and supports Nomura's "diversification gaining pace" thesis. With a single house, the consensus picture is necessarily narrow; no prior TP exists in pdfdata, so there is no formal revision trail to read. Nomura's implied upside from likely current levels (₹2,200–2,400 range) is substantial.

My own read: Sansera is a high-quality, under-followed precision components manufacturer with real optionality beyond its 2W ICE core, but the EV disruption risk is the central question the market is debating. Its 2W powertrain components — connecting rods, camshafts, gear parts — are ICE-specific, and a faster-than-expected shift to electric 2W (Ola, Bajaj Chetak, TVS iQube) would hollow out demand well ahead of its non-auto portfolio growing to compensate. The offsetting thesis — aerospace fasteners and non-auto structural parts — is credible but slower to scale. A 19.3% EBITDA margin in a forging/machining shop is genuinely excellent and reflects operational discipline; that quality should hold valuation support even in a transition. The two things I'd watch most: (1) non-2W revenue share reaching 30%+ (currently tracking ~20–25%), which would materially de-risk the BEV disruption narrative; and (2) any concrete aerospace OEM order wins, which given the multiples aerospace suppliers command could be a step-change re-rating catalyst.

Nomura|260521.change: Buy maintained at ₹3,114; no prior TP on record to compare.
Nomura|260521.view:
Nomura's Buy at ₹3,114 is issued without a prior target to anchor against, so the directional signal is clear but the conviction sizing is harder to assess. The 4QFY26 beat is substantial — +28% revenue and a 190bp EBITDA margin beat above consensus don't happen by accident in a component company — and validates that the diversification effort is real, not just management narrative. Nomura's title "diversification gaining pace" is apt; the question is whether the pace is fast enough to offset ICE-2W secular softening over a 3–5 year horizon.

I'd treat the ₹3,114 target as directionally right but acknowledge wide confidence intervals given single-broker coverage and no TP revision history. A second covering house (domestic or global) picking up Sansera would itself be a positive signal — the stock's relatively low sell-side coverage is part of why the valuation gap to peers may exist. Worth monitoring quarterly: the non-auto and aerospace revenue line items are the key disclosures to track against the thesis.

Shyam Metalics & Energy.summary:
Only **Jefferies** covers Shyam Metalics in the library — a lone bull. The May-31 note raised PT ₹970→₹1,040 and reiterated Buy after a standout Mar-Q (EBITDA +49% QoQ, 18% beat). The debate is not house-vs-house here; the real question is whether the margin expansion that powered the beat is structural — driven by mix shift toward value-added ferro alloys and stainless steel — or partly one-quarter noise. Jefferies’ 14% EPS CAGR FY26–29 thesis rests on doubling carbon-steel capacity and building India’s #3 stainless-steel platform by FY30, an ambitious execution bar in a sector that punishes capex overruns.

My own read: Shyam Metalics is genuinely differentiated for a mid-cap metals name. Its ferroalloys division provides stable, margin-accretive volume tied to domestic EAF steelmakers plus some export, which buffers the inherent cyclicality of the long-steel book. The stainless-steel ambition is the bigger bet: India’s per-capita SS consumption is well below China’s, and import substitution is a real tailwind as domestic capacity builds. But the capex cycle is steep — SS furnaces and cold-rolling mills cost real money, and the company will likely commit ₹3,000–4,000 Cr+ over three years. If HRC/ferroalloy spreads compress simultaneously, free cash flow gets squeezed. Valuation at 8.4x FY27E EV/EBITDA sounds reasonable if margins hold, but steel multiples deserve a cyclicality discount. Two things to watch: the monthly trend in domestic ferroalloy realisations (bellwether for segment margins) and the actual capital spend rate on the SS facility vs plan — any meaningful delay is free cash flow positive short-term but calls the FY30 story into question.

Jeff|260531.view:
Jefferies is the sole sell-side voice here, and the upgrade is clearly results-driven: the Mar-Q beat was large enough (18% EBITDA surprise) to force a 10–17% EPS revision. The reiterated Buy and 14% EPS CAGR outlook is reasonable if the margin expansion was structural — Jefferies implicitly assumes it was. What the note does not stress-test is the execution risk on the stainless-steel capacity build, nor does it model the working capital bleed that a major new-segment ramp typically requires.

At 8.4x FY27E EV/EBITDA the stock is not cheap for a mid-cap Indian metals name with a heavy capex programme, though it is not egregiously valued either. The more useful question is whether this is a “results reaction” re-rating or a durable re-rate on the FY30 capacity/SS story. Jefferies is clearly arguing the latter — credible, but contingent on management capital-allocation discipline holding through the ramp.

Siemens Energy India.summary:
Only **JPMorgan** covers Siemens Energy India in the library, sitting at Neutral. The May-18 note nudged PT marginally from ₹2,600→₹2,650 while maintaining the rating, against a CMP of ₹3,086 at the time — implying roughly 14% downside. JP’s concerns are structural: (1) ENRIN’s HVDC positioning is VSC-only while India’s large transmission projects have historically favoured LCC format, which JP sees as shrinking the addressable HVDC TAM; (2) the industrial-grade gas turbine portfolio grows more slowly than T&D capex broadly. Export wins are the bullish offset JP acknowledges but finds insufficient to upgrade. There is no bull counter-voice in the library — this is a one-sided, methodically argued cautious stance.

My own read: Siemens Energy India is a genuinely unusual animal in the Indian capital goods universe — it is essentially the Indian outpost of Siemens Energy AG’s power-generation and grid-technology businesses, giving it a global order funnel that pure-play domestic names lack. The VSC-vs-LCC HVDC debate is legitimate but nuanced: VSC is the preferred technology globally for renewable integration and offshore grid applications; if India’s upcoming projects (notably 6 GW+ offshore wind evacuation corridors) specify VSC, the TAM concern evaporates and the bull case snaps into focus. That is what the market at ₹3,086 — 14% above target — is partly pricing in. The bear case is that cost-sensitive Indian utilities keep choosing LCC for bulk transmission and ENRIN ends up with a premium-tech product in a price-sensitive market. I’d watch two things above all: (1) the technical format of PGCIL’s upcoming HVDC tender specifications — VSC vs LCC is the single largest swing variable for this stock’s re-rating; and (2) export gas turbine order intake, which is the less-discussed but stabler earnings driver that the sell-side underweights.

JP|260518.view:
JPMorgan’s cautious stance is methodically argued — the HVDC TAM concern and the slow-growth turbine segment are real structural issues, not valuation nitpicks. The stock trading ~14% above target at the time of the note makes the risk-reward clearly unfavourable in JP’s framework, and their relative preference for POWERIND and GVTD implies they see better risk/reward elsewhere in the T&D complex.

The ₹50 PT bump (2,600→2,650) after a headline-beat quarter reads as grudging acknowledgement of the results rather than a genuine change of view — Neutral held, PT barely moved. For a buy-side reader, JP’s value here is the detailed HVDC-technology breakdown. The note is not stale (May 26) and the risk flags are substantive. Discount the Neutral only if you have a firmer read than JP on whether PGCIL’s upcoming HVDC tenders will specify VSC — that is the one lever that could make the bear case wrong.

Sun TV Network.summary:
Only **Kotak** covers Sun TV Network in the local library, having upgraded to **BUY** (from ADD) in May 2026 with a ₹740 target. The upgrade is purely valuation-driven: at the prevailing CMP, the core broadcast business implicitly trades at a *negative* valuation once you assign ₹140bn to the Sunrisers Hyderabad (SRH) IPL franchise and back out ₹78bn of cash. This is a classic SOTP unlock thesis with no other house offering a contrasting view locally — so there is no house debate to adjudicate.

**My own read:** Sun TV is the dominant South Indian broadcaster — particularly Tamil Nadu — but the structural backdrop for linear-TV ad revenue is deteriorating as digital consumption erodes reach. The SOTP argument is intellectually tidy but rests on two shaky legs: SRH's ₹140bn ascribed value is derived from recent franchise deals in an illiquid private market, not a realised cash event; and the cash pile (₹78bn) has historically been hoarded rather than returned. The real risk the sell-side glosses over is the pace of linear-TV ad revenue decline — if Hindi GEC and regional channels lose pricing power faster than expected, EPS estimates will continue to drift lower. I would want to see either (1) a concrete SRH monetisation event, or (2) a meaningful buyback/special dividend before treating the cash as fully deployable in the SOTP. Until then, the upgrade feels opportunistic rather than thesis-changing. Watch: quarterly ad-revenue trends and any SRH stake-sale or IPO news.

Kotak|260521.change: Upgraded to BUY from ADD; PT unchanged at ₹740. No prior TP to compare (no prevTP differential recorded).
Kotak|260521.view:
Kotak's upgrade is a valuation call, not a fundamental re-acceleration. The core argument — that the broadcast business trades at negative implied value vs. the SRH + cash sum — is arithmetically correct at the current price, but it is not the same as saying the stock will re-rate. For the thesis to work, the market must assign SRH at ₹140bn (a private-market comparable, not a liquid value) and accept that the cash will eventually be unlocked. Kotak's 1-2% EPS cut on lower ad revenues reveals the underlying weakness in the business even as it turns bullish.

I would treat this as a floor-hunting upgrade with a narrow margin of safety. The bull case requires a catalyst — SRH monetisation, buyback, or re-rating — that is not yet visible. In the absence of one, the stock can stay 'cheap' on SOTP for extended periods. The structural decline in linear TV is not priced in if the market starts applying a structural-erosion multiple to the broadcast segment rather than treating it as a zero.

TBO Tek.summary:
Only **Jefferies** covers TBO Tek in the local library, maintaining **BUY** at ₹1,615 after the March 2026 quarter results. The key argument: March disruption from the India-Pakistan conflict masked a strong Jan-Feb, with ex-March LFL GTV/EBITDA growing 27%/62% vs the headline 16%/5%. Recovery is visible and Q1FY27 is expected to be better QoQ and YoY. Growth vectors include luxury travel, AI-powered booking (Voya), and the Classic Collection integration. Working capital outflow was flagged as timing-related, not structural. With no competing local house view, there is no internal debate to resolve.

**My own read:** TBO Tek is a well-positioned B2B travel distribution platform with genuine network effects — connecting a large base of travel agents globally with suppliers across hotels and airlines. The asset-light model and India-HQ global reach are differentiated. That said, the long-term disintermediation risk from direct-booking and OTA bypass is real and structurally unresolved. The March disruption was transitory, but the pattern of margin recovery being 'delayed but coming' is now in its second or third iteration, which erodes credibility. The Voya (AI) and Classic (luxury) initiatives are strategically sensible but pre-revenue enough that they are currently narratives rather than earnings. I would watch: (1) Q1FY27 GTV growth rate — does the 'recovery underway' claim hold in the actual print? (2) EBITDA margin trajectory — if SG&A growth has truly moderated, margins should inflect; a third delay would be a red flag. At ₹1,615 TP, Jefferies is pricing a fairly clean recovery.

Jeff|260601.change: PT unchanged at ₹1,615; BUY maintained. prevCall and prevTP both BUY / ₹1,615 — no change.
Jeff|260601.view:
Jefferies' note is essentially a 'hold your nerve' note after a weather event. The ex-March 27%/62% GTV/EBITDA growth is the number that matters, and it is strong. The working capital point is important — if WC normalises in Q1FY27 as claimed, the free cash flow profile improves materially.

My reservation is the recurring 'margin recovery delayed' theme. Jefferies notes SG&A growth has moderated, but the actual EBITDA margin expansion keeps slipping forward. If the Classic integration and Voya investment continue to weigh on costs, the earnings compounding story is less powerful than the buy thesis implies. I'd give Jefferies credit for the transitory disruption call, but I'd want the Q1FY27 numbers before treating the recovery as confirmed rather than anticipated.

TCI Express.summary:
Only **Jefferies** covers TCI Express in the current houseViews set, with a **Buy** but a materially cut target (₹805→₹635). The TP cut reflects a moderated recovery outlook: after positive momentum from Sep-25Q, management turned cautious in Mar-26Q, citing inflation headwinds and lowering FY27E volume growth guidance from ~15% to **10%+ YoY**; Jun-26Q guidance was single-digit growth. The stock was trading near -1SD of historical valuations at the time of the note — pessimism baked in, but not yet a clear re-rating catalyst. There is no second house to disagree with, so the only real debate is between Jefferies' bull case and the market's scepticism.

**My own read:** TCI Express is one of the few pure-play B2B express logistics franchises in India — asset-light model, strong SME/mid-corporate positioning, and historically high return ratios. Three years of near-flat volumes (FY24–26) is the central concern: it reflects macro softness, post-COVID customer-mix shifts, and competitive pressure from organised players like Delhivery's B2B segment. The inflationary squeeze on EBITDA margins (fuel, manpower) makes the recovery path more fragile than Jefferies' headline Buy implies. I'd watch two things above all: (1) whether volume growth actually inflects to 10%+ in H2 FY27 or slips again toward single-digit, and (2) whether pricing power returns — margin recovery depends on it more than volume does. At -1SD valuation, the stock is not obviously a value trap if volumes genuinely recover, but the risk/reward is asymmetric: poor execution will re-rate it down further, while a solid recovery may already be partially priced in at a higher level.

Jeff|260529.view:
Jefferies' cut is an honest mark-to-market on a delayed recovery curve — they stayed bullish on the franchise quality but acknowledged the timeline to full volume and margin recovery is longer than originally modelled. The -1SD valuation note is the closest thing to a 'risk/reward improving' flag in the report, which is fair given where the stock sits.

I'd treat the Buy with moderate conviction: the franchise is real and the downside at current valuations is reasonably bounded, but the upside catalyst — sustained volume re-acceleration above 10% YoY — looks like an H2 FY27 story at best. If Jun-26Q volumes print at the low end of single-digit guidance, another TP cut is likely and the bull case gets pushed out further.

TCS.summary:
Only **Kotak** appears in the current houseViews set, with a **Buy** (TP ₹3,100, unchanged) and a neutral direction tag. The note is a subsidiary-level snapshot focused on TCS's AI-led transformation path: key subplots include a top-account ramp-down dragging TCS e-Serve International, transition-related drag in the Postbank engagement (TCS Technology Solutions GmbH), and the 26× EV/EBITDA Coastal Cloud acquisition — each adding near-term noise around what is otherwise a consensus-Buy name. Morgan Stanley ran a Tactical Idea (OW, TP ₹2,880) that was closed in Jun-26, reflecting that the short-term tactical setup had played out. With only one formal house view and both TP and call unchanged, the real question is whether the AI narrative can sustain current multiples through a patch of top-client and deal-cycle headwinds.

**My own read:** TCS is the highest-quality Indian IT franchise by most measures — deep vertical diversification, sticky multi-year client relationships, and the balance sheet to invest through cycles. The AI-transformation pivot is a genuine medium-term revenue opportunity (services re-architecture, cloud migration, agent-layer build-outs), but it compresses near-term discretionary budgets as clients reorganise spend patterns. The top-account drag is a specific BFSI/BPO headwind that is unlikely to resolve quickly. At the TP cluster around ₹2,880–3,100, the stock is priced for a mid-cycle recovery rather than a structural re-rating. I'd watch top-10 client concentration trends and BFSI deal signing momentum most closely — those two data points tell you more about TCS's FY27 trajectory than any AI narrative, and both are deteriorating or at best flat right now.

Kotak|260526.change: PT ₹3,100→₹3,100; Buy maintained — TP and call both unchanged.
Kotak|260526.view:
Kotak's note reads more as a structural briefing on TCS's subsidiary dynamics than a fresh conviction call — unchanged TP and rating with an AI-transformation framing that applies generically to the sector. The observation about the 26× EV/EBITDA Coastal Cloud acquisition is the sharpest insight: it flags a capital-discipline question that the market is broadly ignoring.

I'd weight this note as a reasonable baseline Buy on a quality compounder, but with limited incremental signal. The lack of any TP move despite identifiable near-term headwinds (top-account ramp-down, Postbank transition drag) implies Kotak is treating these as transient and manageable — which may be right over 12–18 months, but leaves the call somewhat complacent about the path of FY27 earnings revision risk. I'd want to see deal TCV recovering before adding conviction to the Buy.

Tata Comm.summary:
Only **CLSA** covers Tata Comm in the current house-views set, so there is no inter-house debate — the frame is simply one bull thesis. CLSA has a ₹2,600 PT (~37% upside from May 2026 levels of ~₹1,900) and Outperform, anchored on new CEO **Abhijit Panse**'s pivot to profitable growth and digital services acceleration (+19% YoY, +9% QoQ). Digital services are already 50% of data revenue and 43% of total; the bull case is that this mix keeps lifting and the CEO narrative crystallises into margin expansion.

My own read: Tata Comm is a real infrastructure play on India's enterprise digitisation — the 86% data-revenue mix, global MPLS backbone, and managed-security/IoT layering are genuinely differentiated versus domestic telcos. But enterprise networking is a structurally commoditising space: SD-WAN, hyperscaler-native connectivity, and price competition from global integrators all compress B2B margins over time. The new CEO narrative is early-days; without evidence of sustainable EBITDA margin expansion (not just revenue growth), the 37% upside target looks aggressive. I'd watch two things above all: (1) digital-services EBITDA margin, not just revenue growth — the premium to valuation only holds if margin follows; (2) whether the low free float (24%) is amplifying the re-rating story beyond fundamentals.

CLSA|260521.change: OP maintained; prevTP in source data shows ₹104, which is a clear parsing artifact for a stock trading at ₹1,349–1,971 — no reliable prior PT to compare. Call direction (OP) unchanged.
CLSA|260521.view:
CLSA is leaning heavily on the CEO-change catalyst and the digital-services growth vector. The ₹2,600 PT is the most aggressive plausible interpretation of the earnings model — it assumes the profitable-growth pivot actually translates into margin expansion, not just a headline revenue story. The +19% YoY / +9% QoQ digital-services print is the strongest datapoint in the note and it's credible.

What I'd discount: the PT is set well above the 12-month high (₹1,971), so CLSA is effectively calling a new range breakout on execution delivery. That's a high bar for a company mid-CEO transition. The note is light on margin assumptions and heavy on growth narrative — I'd want to see their EBITDA bridge before taking the full ₹2,600 seriously. Useful as a directional bull signal; hold the specific PT loosely.

Tata Consumer Products.summary:
Both **Jefferies** (PT ₹1,450, Buy) and **JPMorgan** (PT ₹1,340, OW) are constructive — no bear voice in the house-views set. Targets are ₹110 apart (Jefferies more optimistic), and neither has moved them recently (both PTs and calls unchanged vs prior). Jefferies approaches the story bottom-up via FY26 annual report execution quality; JPMorgan takes a CEO-guided top-down read from the fireside chat series, emphasising double-digit FY27 revenue confidence. The real question — whether the growth portfolio (NourishCo, Soulfull, Sampann) can scale to 35%+ of India revenue without margin dilution — is where the two implicit models diverge, though neither is openly bearish on it.

My own read: Tata Consumer is a quality FMCG compounder with a credible long-term thesis: Tata brand equity, tea+salt cash-generative core funding growth investments, and premiumisation across health/nutrition. But the sell-side is somewhat glossing over two structural risks. First, **tea** is under secular pressure (urban per-capita consumption declining, input prices volatile); it is the engine funding the growth portfolio but also the earnings swing-factor. Second, the growth businesses (still ~30% of India revenue) need sustained investment before they reach profitability scale — the margin narrative assumes they get there without a period of meaningful drag. At ~60x trailing earnings, a lot of this optionality is priced in. I'd watch: (1) gross margin trajectory — tea-leaf cost and palmolein (Sampann) are the swing factors; (2) whether growth business revenue crosses 35% of India mix with stable or improving margins, which would validate the re-rating story.

JP|260527.view:
The CEO fireside-chat format means this is management-guided messaging, not independent research. D'Souza's confidence in double-digit FY27 revenue and ~30% growth in growth businesses is useful colour but should be taken as a management target, not a forecast. JPMorgan's OW at ₹1,340 is the more conservative of the two bulls — implying they believe the story but with less conviction on the growth portfolio outperformance.

I'd treat this note as a directional sentiment check rather than a thesis update. The key useful signal is that consumer sentiment has stayed stable — that's genuinely reassuring given the macro backdrop. But for a PT revision or thesis change, I'd wait for a proper earnings note with operating leverage evidence.

Jeff|260602.view:
Jefferies' annual-report-analysis angle is the more analytically interesting of the two notes — it looks at execution quality (premiumisation discipline, innovation-distribution-sourcing coordination, alternate channels) rather than just management guidance. The FY26 characterisation as an 'execution-led inflection' is meaningful if it holds: it would mean the growth portfolio is starting to compound, not just grow.

The ₹1,450 PT is the higher of the two and implies Jefferies is comfortable assigning full value to the growth portfolio optionality now. That's a credible stance if gross margins hold — but I'd want to see Q1 FY27 gross margins before fully endorsing it. Jefferies is the more useful counterweight to JPMorgan here: bottom-up execution focus vs. top-down CEO narrative. Both point the same direction, which is the bull case.

United Spirits.summary:
Two houses are in coverage here: **CLSA** (Hold, ₹1,285) is the cautious voice, flagging a concrete near-term cost headwind of 1.25–1.5% of sales in 1QFY27 from elevated glass and crude prices following the Middle East conflict, plus persistent East and Maharashtra volume drags (volumes –5.6% YoY in 4QFY26). **Kotak** (Add, ₹1,480, TP marginally raised from ₹1,450) is the bull, anchoring on 280bps EBITDA margin expansion to 20% and the premiumisation trajectory of UNSP's Prestige & Above (P&A) portfolio. The live pdfdata also shows JPMorgan (OW, ₹1,510 raised from ₹1,445) and Nomura (Buy, ₹1,500 cut from ₹1,650) with May-2026 reports, widening the target cluster to ₹1,285–₹1,510; the bulls appear comfortable looking through the near-term cost hit while CLSA is not. The real debate: whether premiumisation mix shifts can sustainably absorb input cost volatility, or whether the 5.6% volume decline signals demand fragility in a market still dependent on regulatory price hikes for revenue growth.

My own read: Diageo India is one of the highest-quality consumer franchises in the market — entrenched brand equity, secular premiumisation tailwind, and the ability to compel price over time. But the 4QFY26 print shows the limits: volume was negative, price carried the revenue line, and the forthcoming 1QFY27 margin headwind from Middle East pass-through costs is not yet in consensus. The Nomura TP cut (₹1,650→₹1,500) alongside a maintained Buy is a tell — even the bulls are trimming numbers. At current levels I'd watch two things above all: (1) whether 1QFY27 EBITDA margin actually takes the full 1.25–1.5% hit or management can offset with mix, and (2) how quickly Maharashtra regulatory headwinds resolve, since MH is the largest state for spirits. CLSA's ₹1,285 Hold already embeds this caution; the stock is likely range-bound until the cost pass-through cycle clears.

CLSA|260518.change: Dated May-2026; no prior TP on record in pdfdata. Hold maintained at ₹1,285.
CLSA|260518.view:
CLSA's Hold at ₹1,285 is the most conservative in coverage — roughly 14% below Kotak's ₹1,480 and 25% below JPMorgan's ₹1,510. The note is anchored on two real near-term negatives: (1) the Middle East war driving glass and crude prices elevated, translating to a 1.25–1.5% of sales cost headwind in 1QFY27, and (2) ongoing Maharashtra regulatory issues plus East weakness dragging volumes. These are legitimate concerns, not caution for its own sake.

The ₹1,285 target, however, suggests CLSA is not giving full credit to UNSP's structural premiumisation story. The stock's re-rating over the last three years has been driven precisely by the gross margin improvement as P&A volume share rises — and that story hasn't broken. CLSA's Hold is the right near-term call for a 1–2 quarter window; watch whether it upgrades once 1QFY27 numbers confirm the cost headwind was temporary and margins recover. The TP implies limited downside but limited near-term upside too.

Kotak|260518.view:
Kotak's Add with a modest TP raise reflects incremental confidence rather than an aggressive re-rating call. The 280bps EBITDA margin expansion to 20% in 4QFY26 is the anchor of their bull case — gross margin improvement driven by a better P&A mix is exactly the structural driver Diageo India has been executing on since the Covid reset. The ₹1,480 TP is at the lower end of the bull cluster (JPMorgan is at ₹1,510, Nomura at ₹1,500).

The risk I'd probe: P&A value growth of 5% but volume growth of only –3% YoY suggests the mix improvement is being driven by price, not genuine trading-up by consumers. If macro stress in urban India compresses discretionary spend, the premiumisation engine could stall faster than Kotak's model assumes. The ₹1,480 target looks reasonable for a base case but assumes a clean pass-through of costs in 1QFY27 that CLSA explicitly doubts. I'd treat this as a valid bull case contingent on 1QFY27 margin delivery.

Uno Minda.summary:
Three houses are bullish — **Nomura** (Buy, ₹1,494), **CLSA** (Outperform, ₹1,469, TP cut from ₹1,575), **Jefferies** (Buy, ₹1,350, TP unchanged, EPS trimmed 3–4%) — against a sole contrarian bear: **Kotak** (Sell, ₹1,000, TP cut from ₹1,050). Against a CMP of ~₹1,083 (4 June 2026), the target spread is enormous — ₹1,000 to ₹1,494, or roughly –8% to +38%. The consensus among the bulls is that Uno Minda will continue to outperform OEM production volumes through content-per-vehicle gains (access systems, lighting, alloys, infotainment, EV components) and new customer/export wins. **Nomura's June 4 NIFA investor meeting** (the freshest note) is the most important datapoint: management confirmed healthy near-term demand, no production disruption fallout, and highlighted market share gains in existing segments plus new customers in new ones. Kotak's counter — 5% EBITDA miss on gross margin and the expectation that margins will remain range-bound — is the real bear thesis; CLSA and Jefferies both trimmed numbers yet stayed bullish, suggesting the margin weakness is acknowledged but viewed as temporary.

My own read: Uno Minda is one of the better-quality auto component names in India — genuinely diversified across vehicle types, product categories, and increasingly EV platforms. The FY26 track record of 1.5x revenue growth versus 11% OEM volume growth is not an accident; it reflects real content addition. Kotak's SELL at ₹1,000 prices in structural margin compression, but the evidence base is one weak gross margin quarter — a thin basis for a ₹1,000 target when Jefferies sees 24% EPS CAGR over FY26-28. That said, the CLSA TP cut from ₹1,575 to ₹1,469 is worth watching; if we see another round of TP cuts from the bulls in 1QFY27 results, it would suggest the margin story is more persistent than the bears claim. My two watches: (1) quarterly gross margin trend — is it bottoming or still deteriorating? and (2) EV order win disclosures — Jefferies flagged new EV parts orders, and crystallisation of these into revenue is the key re-rating catalyst.

Nomura|260604.change: PT unchanged at ₹1,494; Buy maintained. Most recent note (4 Jun 2026) — post-NIFA investor conference.
Nomura|260604.view:
Nomura's June 4 note is qualitatively the most important in this set because it is the freshest and follows a direct management interaction at Nomura Investment Forum Asia. The confirmation that near-term demand is healthy and there is no production disruption impact from the India-Pakistan conflict is a genuine data point, not just a reiteration of prior thesis.

The ₹1,494 Buy (38% upside from CMP) is the highest target in coverage and implies Nomura is not just tactically constructive but sees a meaningful revaluation opportunity. The incremental colour on 'new customers in new segments' and 'strong potential export growth levers' is worth taking seriously — Uno Minda has been quietly expanding its global OEM relationships, and if exports scale, the market is not pricing it. I'd weight Nomura's view heavily here, precisely because it is the most current and management-informed.

CLSA|260518.view:
CLSA's TP cut is a recalibration, not a thesis change. The 'another steady quarter' framing captures the reality: 4QFY26 was in-line with expectations, FY26 delivered 1.5x revenue growth vs OEM volumes — the content-per-vehicle outperformance story is intact. The ₹1,469 Outperform still implies ~36% upside from the June CMP.

The TP cut signals CLSA is baking in slightly lower near-term margin assumptions, consistent with Jefferies' EPS trim and Kotak's gross margin concern. The key question is whether further TP cuts follow in 1QFY27 results; if CLSA moves toward ₹1,300–₹1,350, it would start converging toward Jefferies and the bull cluster would compress. For now, CLSA's stance is constructive with appropriate near-term humility on margins.

Jeff|260518.change: PT unchanged at ₹1,350; Buy maintained. FY27-28E EPS trimmed 3–4%.
Jeff|260518.view:
Jefferies' decision to hold its ₹1,350 Buy despite cutting estimates 3–4% reflects confidence that the structural growth story overrides near-term margin noise. A 24% EPS CAGR over FY26-28 — even after the trim — is a powerful number for an auto component stock. The EV parts order wins mentioned in the Jefferies summary are an incremental positive that the market may not fully be pricing.

The EPS trim is still a flag: Jefferies is acknowledging margin pressure, not dismissing it. If FY28E EPS gets cut more than ~10% in aggregate from here, the ₹1,350 TP would need revisiting. I'd treat the Jefferies Buy as credible but watch whether they pull the TP down toward Kotak's ₹1,000–₹1,100 territory in the next results cycle.

Kotak|260518.view:
Kotak's Sell at ₹1,000 — below the CMP of ₹1,083 — is the strongest contrarian call in coverage. The 'lackluster quarter' thesis rests on a 5% EBITDA miss driven by gross margin weakness, and Kotak's expectation that margins will remain range-bound is the structural bear argument. The TP cut from ₹1,050 to ₹1,000 is modest but directionally consistent.

I'd be sceptical of the Kotak Sell as a standalone call for several reasons: (1) the other three houses — including a June 4 post-management-meeting note from Nomura — are all bullish and see demand as healthy; (2) the stock is already trading at a significant discount to the bull cluster (₹1,350–₹1,494), which implies the market has already partially priced in margin risk; and (3) Kotak expects industry outperformance on content gains (they explicitly say so) — the only disagreement is on margin, not on top-line trajectory. A range-bound margin at 14–15% EBITDA is not catastrophic if revenue is growing 15%+. Kotak's view is worth monitoring as the minority bear, but the risk/reward of following it at CMP looks asymmetric to the downside.

Varroc Engineering.summary:
Only **Kotak** covers Varroc Engineering here, with a bear direction and a REDUCE rating. The absence of bull voices makes this less a debate and more a single-house verdict: the domestic auto-components business is underperforming on both revenue and margins, and competitive intensity in EV components is structural, not cyclical. The PT cut from ₹2,026 to ₹550 is dramatic — most likely this reflects a post-demerger reset (the international lighting business was separated), meaning the old target priced a different, larger entity; but even on a like-for-like domestic basis the revision signals deep scepticism about near-term recovery. The B2B nature of the business and two-wheeler OEM pricing power over vendors limits Varroc's ability to offset margin pressure.

My own read: Varroc Engineering's domestic rump — focused on two-wheeler auto-electricals, polymers and lighting — is a structurally weaker business than the pre-demerger entity. The EV orderbook is real, but converting EV content wins to margin in a segment where OEMs (Bajaj, TVS, Hero) are aggressively squeezing the supply chain is the core execution challenge. I would not lean against Kotak's scepticism here. What I'd watch: (1) EV revenue as a share of total sales and its gross margin vs ICE mix; (2) working-capital trends — auto-component companies tend to bleed cash when revenue disappoints; (3) whether a second broker initiates coverage with a materially different view, which would signal that the bear case is being re-examined.

Kotak|260528.change: PT slashed ₹2,026→₹550; REDUCE maintained. Q4 PAT of ₹2.2 bn was 6% below estimates on a weak revenue print.
Kotak|260528.view:
Kotak's call is internally consistent: they're not wavering on REDUCE even after a large PT cut, which suggests conviction rather than indecision. The magnitude of the PT reset (−73%) is striking — this appears tied to a post-demerger recalibration of the addressable earnings base, not just a cyclical miss. Their emphasis on competitive intensity in the EV segment is the most useful insight: as OEMs deepen their EV component in-sourcing or diversify vendors, Varroc's content-per-vehicle economics could erode before the EV volume ramp compensates.

I'd take the REDUCE seriously. The one thing I'd push back on is the framing of EV orderbook growth as unambiguously positive — orderbook wins at sub-par margins are a revenue tailwind but a margin headwind, and Kotak acknowledges this. The bear case is well-grounded.

Varun Beverages.summary:
All three covering houses — **Jefferies** (BUY, TP ₹615), **Kotak** (ADD, TP ₹540) and **MorganStanley** (ADD, no TP in this note) — are constructive, so the debate here is about *how much* optionality to price in, not whether to own the stock. The galvanising event is the PepsiCo franchise renegotiation: VBL's India bottling agreement has been extended to April 2049 (from April 2039) and, crucially, the clause restricting VBL to operating solely as PepsiCo's Indian SPV has been removed. This transforms the investment case from a high-quality bottler to a potential diversified F&B platform. Jefferies' TP (₹615) vs Kotak's (₹540) likely reflects different assumptions about how and when VBL monetises the new latitude. MorganStanley's June conference note adds a near-term data point: management expects Q2 to outpace Q1 on a weak 2025 base, with double-digit volume growth targeted over the medium term.

My own read: VBL is a genuine quality franchise — Jaipuria-group execution has been among the best in India's consumer space — and the franchise extension is a real, durable positive. The removal of the non-compete restriction is optionality, but I'd be disciplined about pricing it in. Building a second F&B vertical from scratch is capital-intensive, and management has no track record outside PepsiCo. The stock likely already prices in a good chunk of the optimism. What I'd watch most: (1) actual Q2 volume and realisation vs the bullish management guidance; (2) packing material cost headwinds mentioned by MorganStanley — compressed margins in a hot-summer quarter would be a yellow flag; (3) any concrete signal on non-PepsiCo category strategy. The risk the sell-side is underplaying is execution complexity if VBL pursues multiple fronts simultaneously.

MorganStan|260603.change: Conference note — no TP cited; ADD maintained. No prior TP in pdfdata to compare.
MorganStan|260603.view: This is a management-meeting feedback note rather than a formal initiation or estimate revision, so the analytical weight is limited. The useful takeaways are directional: management is confident about Q2 volume acceleration on a weak base, and packing-material inventory has been covered at elevated cost — which is a near-term margin drag worth watching. Morgan Stanley's ADD without a cited TP in this note makes it hard to gauge how aggressively they're underwriting the optionality thesis.

Kotak|260522.change: PT ₹540→₹540 (unchanged); ADD maintained. Report focused on the revised PepsiCo franchise agreement — no estimate revision triggered.
Kotak|260522.view:
Kotak's 'VBL Uncapped' framing neatly captures the strategic shift: the removal of the SPV restriction is the more important clause, not just the tenure extension. Their ADD at ₹540 is more conservative than Jefferies' ₹615, implying they're assigning less immediate value to the optionality — a defensible stance given that execution of any non-PepsiCo category is years away.

I find Kotak's measured reaction appropriate: they see the franchise extension as materially positive for long-term strategic flexibility without rushing to price in a diversification scenario that has no timeline or details yet. The ₹540 ADD is a quality-franchise call, not an optionality bet.

Jeff|260521.change: PT ₹615→₹615 (unchanged); BUY maintained. Quick take on franchise renegotiation — no estimate revision.
Jeff|260521.view:
Jefferies is the most bullish of the three with the highest TP (₹615), and their framing of 'Longer Franchise, Larger Optionality' is the clearest articulation of the bull case. They are honest that the details of any non-PepsiCo category moves 'are not yet clear' — which means the ₹615 BUY is partly a quality-of-franchise premium call and partly a bet on management's capital-allocation track record.

That premium is probably warranted given VBL's operational history, but I'd want to see management explicitly commit to (or clearly rule out) near-term category expansion before giving full credit. Jefferies' ₹75 gap over Kotak's TP is the cleanest expression of the optionality-pricing debate between the houses.

Vinati Organics.summary:
Only **Kotak** covers Vinati Organics in the current houseViews, and they are firmly bearish — SELL with FV ₹1,200 (trimmed from ₹1,260), underpinned by a further 9–10% EPS cut. There is no bull counterweight in the local library, and no external Trendlyne entries either, so the picture is one-directional. The core concern: **IBB and ATBS** drove a 1% revenue decline in FY26, VOPL projects continue to underperform, and management's 15% volume growth guidance for FY27 looks aspirational given the run of downward revisions.

My own read: Vinati has historically been an exceptional specialty-chemicals franchise — clean balance sheet, high ROCE, strong product moats in IBB and ATBS. But the FY26 performance makes clear that the China re-opening has materially changed the competitive landscape for both key molecules, and the VOPL diversification is absorbing capital without yet delivering offsetting revenue. The pattern of consecutive EPS cuts is the tell: this is not a one-quarter blip but a cycle where estimates keep chasing the reality lower. I'd land closer to Kotak than the bulls; the 15% volume target is achievable only if IBB/ATBS spot pricing firms simultaneously — which is the variable to watch most. The second thing to watch is VOPL project timelines and whether capex absorption accelerates ahead of any cash contribution.

Kotak|260528.change: FV cut ₹1,260 → ₹1,200; SELL maintained; EPS trimmed 9–10%.
Kotak|260528.view:
Kotak's bear case is well-grounded. The FY26 revenue decline from IBB/ATBS weakness is not a one-off — it reflects structural pricing pressure and rising competition, and the 9–10% EPS reduction is in a series of consecutive downward revisions to estimates. This pattern of persistent degradation is more worrying than any single miss.

The VOPL project struggles add a new layer of risk: capex is being absorbed without revenue uplift, which compresses near-term ROCE. I'd stress the 15% volume guidance harder than Kotak does — Vinati has a strong track record of execution, but the competitive environment has genuinely changed since FY22–23. IBB/ATBS spot pricing and any VOPL commissioning update at the FY27 Q1 call are the two pivots for reassessing.

Vodafone Idea.summary:
All four covered houses are bearish or cautious: **JPMorgan** and **Kotak** both carry UW/SELL at ₹9; **CLSA** is Underperform at ₹13; **Nomura** downgraded from Buy to Neutral and raised TP to ₹12.6. Targets cluster tightly at ₹9–13, implying the stock is at or past fair value even after the twin positives — government AGR relief (₹877bn → ₹640bn) and ABG promoter infusion (₹47.3bn warrants at ₹11/share). The key debate is not direction (everyone is cautious) but whether the funding relief is enough to fund the capex Vi needs to stop bleeding subscribers to Jio and Airtel. Nomura was the one bull in the room and has just moved to Neutral; JPMorgan flagged near-term bank-funding constraints as the real gating risk.

My own read: The AGR recategorisation and ABG warrant commitment are genuine positives — they reduce existential risk and buy time. But they do not solve the structural problem: Vi's ₹174 ARPU still lags Airtel (₹200+) and increasingly Jio (₹180+), its 5G rollout is underfunded, and the 75% of ABG warrants not yet called leaves a large deferred capital gap. The subscriber base stabilisation in Q4FY26 (0.1m loss vs 5.3m in 9M) is the one encouraging datapoint, but it needs to hold for several quarters to be conclusive. The 3-year EBITDA target Kotak flags as ambitious would require Vi to simultaneously arrest subscriber churn, drive ARPU higher, and expand margins — all in a market where Jio and Airtel have structural cost advantages. I'd watch two things above all: whether bank credit lines open post-government relief (JPMorgan's key variable), and whether the 75% ABG warrant conversion actually materialises on schedule. Until those two are resolved, the risk-reward at current prices is poor.

CLSA|260519.change: Underperform maintained; TP ₹13. Prior TP in pdfdata (₹108) is a parsing artefact — no reliable prior to compare.
CLSA|260519.view:
CLSA's ₹13 TP is the highest among the four houses yet still carries an Underperform — a notable combination. Their focus on the AGR present-value gain as a one-time PAT boost (₹520bn reported PAT in 4QFY26) correctly separates the accounting benefit from the operating reality: the cash-flow position improves from reduced scheduled payments, but EBITDA generation is unchanged.

The promoter infusion is treated as a marginal positive — credible as a signal of ABG commitment but not transformational given the scale of Vi's funding needs. I'd align with CLSA's cautious framing: the accounting win flatters the headline numbers, and the operating leverage story requires capex that isn't yet funded at scale.

JP|260519.change: PT ₹9; UW maintained; no change vs prior.
JP|260519.view:
JPMorgan's title — 'Not out of the woods yet' — frames the call correctly. The ₹9 TP unchanged despite the positive catalysts signals they see no margin of safety at current prices, and their specific flag on near-term bank funding constraints is the most operationally granular concern raised by any house.

The ABG warrant structure (25% upfront, 75% over 18 months) means the bulk of capital is deferred — and deferral implies conditionality. If Vi's operating metrics deteriorate or the broader macro environment shifts, ABG's willingness to call the remaining warrants could be tested. JPMorgan's UW at ₹9 is arguably the most rigorous bear position in the coverage; I'd put material weight on their bank-credit read.

Kotak|260519.view:
A ₹1 TP bump (12.5%) while holding SELL captures Kotak's view precisely: the government relief and ABG news are incrementally positive but nowhere near sufficient to change the trajectory. Their challenge to the 3-year EBITDA target is the right question — hitting it requires Vi to execute on subscriber stabilisation, ARPU improvement, and margin expansion simultaneously, with constrained capex and against better-funded competitors.

Kotak is the most rigorous structural bear among the four. Their SELL at ₹9 implicitly says the positive newsflow is already priced in, and that the base case still points to value destruction at current multiples. I find this the most credible single-house read.

Nomura|260518.view:
The combination of a downgrade and a TP raise is unusual but interpretable: Nomura's improved ₹12.6 TP reflects the genuine balance-sheet benefit from the AGR present-value recategorisation, while the downgrade to Neutral signals the stock had already run to price in the catalysts. Their focus on ARPU as the key monitorable is correct — it is the one lever Vi can pull without large capex (via tariff discipline and subscriber-mix improvement).

Nomura was the relative bull in this coverage set and has now landed at Neutral. That migration matters: it suggests the positive catalyst cycle from the AGR/ABG news is substantially priced in at current levels. I'd read the downgrade as a more important signal than the TP raise.

Welspun Living.summary:
Only one house appears in local coverage — an unidentified broker (file metadata shows "Unknown") with a Buy and a PT of ₹180, raised from ₹165 after Q4FY26 results. The report characterises the quarter as a sequential recovery with EBITDA and PAT beats despite soft global retail demand, though the simultaneous estimate cuts (PAT -6% for FY27E) temper the enthusiasm. With just one house visible, there is no cross-house debate to map — the picture is singly constructive but the PT implies limited upside, and the broker's identity makes comparability difficult.

My own read: Welspun Living is India's largest home textiles exporter, dominant in terry towels and bed linens, with its revenue overwhelmingly driven by US retail chains (Walmart, Target, Bed Bath & Beyond successors). The Q4FY26 beat is encouraging but the business faces structural headwinds that a one-quarter recovery does not resolve: (1) US tariff and trade policy risk — any India-targeted tariff regime would hit Welspun's export economics directly; (2) competitive pressure from Bangladesh and Vietnam in the value segment, where Welspun does not have a structural cost advantage; (3) heavy customer concentration among a few US mass-market retailers whose own inventory management cycles drive lumpy demand. The bull case rests on the India+1 sourcing shift as US buyers reduce China exposure, and Welspun's vertically integrated scale. I'd want to see two or three quarters of margin stability (EBITDA margins recovering toward 13-14%) before treating the recovery as durable. The ₹180 PT offers modest upside from current levels — the stock is a hold-and-watch rather than a conviction add until the macro headwinds around US trade policy clarify.

Unknown|260518.view:
The Q4FY26 beat on EBITDA and PAT gives the bull case a data point, and the PT raise to ₹180 is a confidence signal. But the simultaneous estimate cuts — revenue -2%, PAT -6% for FY27E — reveal that the broker is not expecting the recovery to be rapid or margin-accretive beyond what is already in the stock. The ₹180 PT implies limited upside from here, making this a Hold-calibre Buy in practice.

The broker's identity being unknown limits how much weight to put on the call. The underlying Q4FY26 data (revenue ₹2,435 Cr, EBITDA beat, PAT beat) is the more useful anchor. I'd discount the PT and focus instead on whether Q1FY27 shows the sequential recovery continuing — if it does, the stock becomes more interesting; if global retail softens further (US consumer confidence, inventory destocking), the FY27E estimates will face another leg of cuts.

Whirlpool of India.summary:
The two houses split sharply in conviction but not in diagnosis. Kotak is Buy (FV ₹1,050, cut from ₹1,180) while Jefferies is Hold (PT ₹850, trimmed marginally from ₹855) — both responding to an ugly Q4FY26 where EBITDA fell 34-41% YoY, driven by the BEE energy-efficiency table change (product transition costs that price hikes failed to fully recover) and raw-material inflation (copper, aluminum, imported compressors). Kotak cut FY27E EPS by ~37% and still holds Buy, betting on management's market-share recovery plan in RAC and front-load WM; Jefferies is more guarded, emphasising that RM cost headwinds and a weak INR are structural near-term risks rather than one-offs. The ₹200 spread between the two PTs (₹1,050 vs ₹850, a ~24% gap) signals genuine disagreement on how quickly margins normalise — this is the live debate in the stock.

My own read: Whirlpool India is in a genuinely difficult position that goes beyond cyclical margin compression. The BEE table change is a regulatory event the whole industry faced, but Whirlpool appears to have under-priced the transition — insufficient price hikes relative to the cost step-up is a management execution failure, not merely bad luck. The imported-compressor exposure (~25-30% of AC BoM per Jefferies) is a structural vulnerability in a weak-INR world, especially since Whirlpool lacks the domestic compressor integration that some peers have. The most concerning signal is the RAC market-share loss: the AC category is India's fastest-growing appliance segment, and being under-indexed while simultaneously managing a product reset is a double disadvantage that takes multiple quarters to fix. I lean closer to Jefferies' cautious Hold. Kotak's Buy is credible only if you trust management's ability to execute the portfolio reset quickly — a reasonable bet in theory, but Whirlpool India's track record on execution has been inconsistent. What I'd watch most closely: (1) AC category market-share data in Q1FY27 (the first quarter after the BEE transition settles) and (2) whether EBITDA margins show any recovery toward 7-8% by H2FY27, from the sub-5% implied by the Q4FY26 print. Until one of those data points lands, the stock feels like a show-me story.

Kotak|260523.change: FV cut ₹1,180→₹1,050; Buy maintained. FY2027/28E EPS cut ~37%/15%.
Kotak|260523.view:
Kotak's Buy through a 37% EPS cut is a bold call — it signals the house believes the pain is transitory and that Whirlpool's brand and distribution can support a margin recovery once the BEE transition and RM inflation headwinds ease. The focus on portfolio gaps (RAC under-indexation, front-load WM) is the right framing: these are fixable operational issues, not structural demand problems.

That said, a 37% EPS cut is large, and maintaining Buy requires strong conviction in the recovery timeline. The ₹1,050 FV still implies ~25% upside from the Jeff PT — suggesting Kotak is pricing in a normalisation scenario that Jefferies is not. I'd treat the Kotak Buy as the optimistic scenario: valid if management executes, but dependent on several things going right simultaneously (RM stability, INR stabilisation, successful new-product launches in RAC). Worth watching for execution signals in H1FY27 before relying on this call.

Jeff|260521.change: PT trimmed ₹855→₹850; Hold maintained. EPS cut 3-4%.
Jeff|260521.view:
Jefferies' 3-4% EPS cut looks mild relative to the scale of the EBITDA miss (-34% YoY), which suggests the house is absorbing near-term pain within an already-cautious valuation rather than revising its medium-term earnings view. The Hold is the honest stance here — the stock is not obviously cheap enough to Buy given the RM headwinds and market share risks, but neither is it a clear Sell if you believe the BEE disruption is a one-year event.

The most useful thing in Jefferies' note is the BoM breakdown for ACs (copper 9-10%, aluminum 2-3%, steel 4-5%, compressor 25-30%) — this gives a concrete framework for sensitivity analysis as commodity and INR moves play out. Jefferies is the better reference for near-term cost pressure tracking; Kotak is more useful for the recovery scenario. At ₹850, the Jefferies PT prices in limited recovery — I'd treat it as a floor estimate, not a central case, if RM and INR stabilise in H2FY27.

Chalet Hotels.summary:
All four active houses are bullish, but conviction and targets diverge sharply. **Kotak** (ADD, PT ₹900) is the most cautious — they cut their target by ₹125 after FY26 results, labelling the year-end "rickety" despite the strong headline. The ADD (not a Buy) signals limited near-term upside confidence. **IDBI** (Buy, PT ₹937) upgraded from Hold to Buy in May 2026, but simultaneously cut the PT from ₹1,025 — a valuation-driven call rather than a fundamental re-rating, essentially saying the stock de-rated enough to justify the switch. **PL** (Buy, PT ₹1,089) and **ICICI** (Buy, PT ₹1,123) are structurally more optimistic, but PL's last note is from Feb 2026 and ICICI's from Nov 2025 — both predate the full FY26 result. The PT spread from lowest (Kotak ₹900) to highest (ICICI ₹1,123) is ~25%, reflecting genuine disagreement on how much credit to give the residential pipeline. The real debate is whether the Manthan/Athiva brand build-out and residential segment are a value-accretive diversification or a complication that distorts the pure hospitality story that the market typically prices on EV/EBITDA.

My own read: Chalet is an interesting hybrid — a premium upscale hotel base in gateway cities (Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune) now grafting on a residential component and an urban boutique brand. The 61% FY26 headline revenue/EBITDA growth is real but misleading: ₹7.4bn of residential recognition is lumpy and completion-driven, not recurring hospitality income. Strip that out and the 18%/21% hotel EBITDA growth is solid but not exceptional within the India hospitality supercycle. I would sit closer to Kotak's cautious ADD than to ICICI's ₹1,123 Buy. The dual-business model adds execution complexity; residential delivery introduces timing risk (delays push recognition out and compress IRR); and the ongoing capacity expansion is capex-heavy. Two things I would watch most: (1) RevPAR trajectory in Q1–Q2 FY27 as new rooms come online — adding supply in a single city can pressure occupancy faster than the macro tailwind can absorb it; (2) pace and margin of residential deliveries under Manthan/Athiva — the market is treating the pipeline as a free call option, but if launches or completions slip, the stock will re-rate quickly to pure-hospitality multiples where the PT range compresses toward ₹800–900.

Kotak|260518.view:
Kotak's headline for this note — "Rickety close to the year" — is the telling signal. They kept the ADD but cut the target by ₹125, which effectively strips out most near-term upside. The residential revenue boost (₹7.4bn recognised in FY26) is the flattering factor in the headline 61% growth, and Kotak is clearly discounting its repeatability.

The ADD rather than Buy reflects a reasonable middle ground: the franchise is good and capacity additions are progressing, but valuations already embed a lot of the hospitality upturn. I find Kotak's disciplined distinction between hospitality EBITDA and residential lumpiness more analytically sound than the bulls who blend the two. Worth taking their downward PT revision seriously given they have the freshest, post-results view.

IDBI|260518.change: Upgraded to Buy from Hold (prior note 06-Nov-2025); PT cut from ₹1,025 to ₹937.
IDBI|260518.view:
This is an unusual combination — a rating upgrade alongside a PT cut. The prior IDBI Hold (Nov 2025, PT ₹1,025) was essentially saying the stock was fairly valued then; the upgrade to Buy now at ₹937 implies the stock fell enough in the interim that the risk/reward flipped even at a lower fundamental target.

That logic is internally consistent but tells you IDBI's upgrade is valuation-driven, not a change in fundamental view. It does not contradict Kotak's concerns about result quality. I would treat the IDBI Buy as a floor-finding call rather than a growth re-rating — useful as a signal that downside is limited around current levels, less useful as evidence of a strong re-rating catalyst ahead.

PL|260224.change: Buy maintained, PT unchanged at ₹1,089 (consistent with their 03-Feb-2026 note at the same level). Note is dated Feb-2026 and predates FY26 full-year results — now somewhat stale.
PL|260224.view:
PL's Feb 2026 "Manthan Hotels" note frames Chalet's evolution as a brand-building and mixed-use story, with TP ₹1,089 implying structural value from the Athiva/Manthan pipeline above and beyond the existing hotel EBITDA. The unchanged TP across their Q3FY26 update (Feb 3) and this thematic note (Feb 24) suggests high conviction at that level.

However, the note is now about 3.5 months old and was written before the FY26 full-year results that prompted Kotak's PT cut. PL's ₹1,089 may not be stale on the thesis, but it has not been stress-tested against the actual FY26 delivery. I would watch for whether PL revises post the FY26 annual results release — if they hold ₹1,089 with updated numbers, that would be genuinely meaningful. For now, treat with moderate discount for staleness.

ICICI|251105.change: PT raised ₹1,058→₹1,123; Buy maintained. Note dated Nov-2025 — approximately 7 months old, predates FY26 results.
ICICI|251105.view:
ICICI holds the highest PT on the street at ₹1,123, anchored to the new Athiva brand rollout and the medium-term asset pipeline thesis they have been consistently building (they raised PT again from ₹1,058 in the Q2FY26 update to ₹1,123 here). Their thesis is coherent: Chalet's pipeline of new hotels plus the branded-residences angle creates a medium-term earnings step-up that current multiples undervalue.

The problem is this note is from November 2025 and is now the stalest of the four active views. Given Kotak — with a fresher FY26 post-results lens — cut their PT by ₹125, ICICI's ₹1,123 looks increasingly like a figure that has not been refreshed to reflect actual delivery. I would discount it as directionally correct on the structural thesis but likely to be trimmed on the next update cycle. The highest PT with the oldest timestamp is a combination to flag.

Coforge.summary:
Five houses covered; three bull (CLSA, PL, ICICI) vs two neutral/hold (IDBI, BOB). The target-price dispersion is extreme: ₹1,300 (IDBI, BOB) vs ₹2,020–₹2,075 (PL, CLSA) — roughly 55% apart — which is unusual for a single Q4 result update cycle and signals genuine valuation disagreement rather than minor methodological differences. CLSA (Jun-2026, post-NDR, freshest) is the most actionable bull at OP/₹2,075 after a small PT nudge from ₹2,026. PL is the strongest Q4 reaction bull (Buy/₹2,020). ICICI upgraded from Hold to Buy in May but cut its PT to ₹1,660 — now well below the market price, making the call functionally stale. Both IDBI and BOB downgraded/held at ₹1,300 post-Q4, calls that have been overtaken by the stock's move; the real debate is whether organic revenue growth reacceleration is durable or a one-quarter story.

My own read: Coforge's franchise quality is solid — its BFS and insurance vertical depth is genuine, not a marketing label, and the AI angle (workflow automation in financial services) is a credible demand driver rather than a re-labelling exercise. CLSA's NDR framing of it as an 'AI cycle winner' is plausible in the near term. That said, at ~₹1,977 the stock has already recovered most of the ground from its 12-month low of ₹1,072, and the re-rating has been fast. What I'd stress-test: (1) organic growth ex-acquisitions — Coforge has been acquisition-heavy and stripping that out is harder than it looks; (2) deal margin sustainability as BFS clients sharpen vendor negotiation; (3) whether management's confident NDR tone is matched by actual Q1FY27 deal TCV and revenue. The hold camp's ₹1,300 TPs are clearly stale, but they contain a real warning: at these valuations any organic growth miss will hurt. I'd lean cautiously constructive, anchoring on CLSA's thesis while watching Q1FY27 organic growth numbers closely.

CLSA|260604.view:
The freshest read in the set — post-NDR management interaction rather than a Q4 result note — and carries more signal than the May result reactions. The AI cycle winner framing is directionally credible for Coforge's BFS/insurance verticals, which are natural AI-consumption plays (workflow automation, underwriting, compliance).

The PT nudge is modest (~2.4%) rather than a conviction upgrade, but the maintained Outperform and above-consensus target suggest CLSA came away from the NDR more comfortable than before. The key risk to this call is that management confidence at NDRs is structurally optimistic; I'd want to see Q1FY27 organic deal TCV before treating this as high-conviction.

ICICI|260506.change: Upgraded from Hold (TP ₹1,880, Dec-2025) to Buy; PT cut to ₹1,660 (May-2026).
ICICI|260506.view:
A technically paradoxical call: the rating was upgraded to Buy while the price target was cut from ₹1,880 to ₹1,660 — almost certainly because the stock had fallen well below its Dec-2025 level by Q4 result day, making the upside to ₹1,660 look buyable at the time. But the stock has since recovered sharply, and ICICI's TP of ₹1,660 is now meaningfully below the prevailing market price, rendering the Buy call effectively obsolete.

The underlying thesis — margins holding the fort, organic revenue growth is the key unlock for the next re-rating leg — is correct framing and worth retaining. But don't treat the 'Buy' rating at face value given the stale PT; ICICI would likely need to revise before this becomes actionable again.

IDBI|260506.change: Downgraded to Hold with TP ₹1,300 (May-2026); no prior IDBI report in library to compare previous PT.
IDBI|260506.view:
IDBI's downgrade was the most contrarian post-Q4 call, and its TP of ₹1,300 is now roughly 34% below market — making it one of the most underwater sell-side calls in the set. The downgrade thesis (organic growth uncertainty, execution risk on deal momentum) was defensible at the time and reflects a legitimate concern the bulls are glossing over.

At current prices this call is operationally obsolete as a trading signal, but it's worth keeping as a bear-case anchor. If Q1FY27 organic growth disappoints and deal TCV momentum stalls, the multiple compression IDBI worried about could still arrive, just from a higher base. Watch IDBI for a revision — if they don't upgrade by Q1FY27 results, they likely still have reservations about the re-rating quality.

PL|260506.change: Buy maintained with TP ₹2,020 (May-2026); no prior PL report in library to compare.
PL|260506.view:
The most grounded Q4 bull reaction: TP ₹2,020 is essentially in line with CLSA's post-NDR target and roughly in line with current market price, implying PL's conviction was not misplaced. The 'strong execution + doubling down on AI' framing matches what CLSA heard at the NDR.

PL is the call I'd take most seriously among the May-2026 result notes — it sits at the constructive end without requiring heroic assumptions, and the focus on AI opportunity is substantive rather than decorative. The main gap vs CLSA is recency: PL's note precedes the NDR management interaction, so CLSA has a more current read on pipeline confidence.

BOB|260506.change: Hold with TP ₹1,300 (May-2026); no prior BOB report in library to compare.
BOB|260506.view:
BOB's 'likely in leaders quadrant on FY27 organic growth' framing is a backhanded compliment — it concedes operational quality while maintaining a TP that is now deeply below market. Like IDBI, this was probably a valuation-discipline call made when the stock was much lower; neither anticipated the pace of recovery.

Useful mainly as a valuation floor reference: BOB's ₹1,300 represents roughly the level at which even a cautious house would expect support. The 'leaders quadrant' language suggests BOB is not bearish on fundamentals — this looks like a valuation overhang concern that has been overtaken by market momentum. Low informational weight at current price levels.

BrainBees Solutions.summary:
Only one house — **Kotak** — covers BrainBees Solutions (FirstCry) in the local library, so there is no cross-house debate to map. Kotak is nominally bull-directioned but cut its price target sharply from ₹430 → ₹350 (~19%) while maintaining Buy in its May 2026 note after 4Q results. The cut reflects margin compression: India EBITDA margin contracted 202 bps yoy to 7.3% on raw-material cost inflation, heavier discounting, and quick-commerce investment. GlobalBees (D2C house-of-brands) grew 15% yoy and is the one outperforming segment; the core India multichannel business grew 11.4% and the international segment 9.5%.

My own read: BrainBees is a structurally interesting bet on India's underpenetrated baby/kids market, but the bull case requires believing that the quick-commerce push will build a defensible moat rather than simply subsidise demand already served more efficiently by Blinkit or Swiggy Instamart. The 202-bps margin contraction in a single quarter is a real warning sign — discounting to defend share while simultaneously absorbing RM inflation and building out q-comm infrastructure is a triple headwind. GlobalBees growing at 15% is the most credible long-term value driver, but it is still small relative to the consolidated P&L. I would want to see India EBITDA margins stabilising (ideally recovering towards 9–10%) before accepting Kotak's Buy at face value. The two things I'd watch most: (1) whether quick-commerce unit economics improve as the network scales, and (2) whether international (largely Middle East) can sustain growth without further discount intensification.

Kotak|260527.change: PT cut ₹430 → ₹350; Buy maintained. Margin estimates trimmed on RM inflation, higher discounting, and quick-commerce investments.
Kotak|260527.view:
Kotak is maintaining a Buy after a material ~19% target cut, which itself telegraphs eroding conviction.
